messages.content: Explain in exactly three sentences why floating-point addition is not associative.
Explain in exactly three sentences why floating-point addition is not associative.

samples.text: Floating‑point numbers have a finite precision, so each operation rounds the exact real result to the nearest representable value. When you add three numbers, rounding after the first addition can change the magnitude of the intermediate sum, causing a different rounding error than if you round after the second addition. Consequently, (a + b) + c and a + (b + c) can produce distinct floating‑point results, breaking associativity.

Floating‑point numbers have a finite precision, so each operation rounds the exact real result to the nearest representable value. When you add three numbers as \((a+b)+c\), the rounding after the first addition can change the magnitude of the intermediate sum, affecting the rounding of the second addition; doing the additions as \(a+(b+c)\) rounds a different intermediate value, leading to a potentially different final result. Because the rounding errors depend on the order of operations, the associative law \((a+b)+c = a+(b+c)\) does not hold for floating‑point arithmetic.

When you add three numbers, the rounding after the first addition can change the magnitude of the intermediate sum, causing a different rounding error than if you add the other two first. Consequently, \((a+b)+c\) and \(a+(b+c)\) can produce different floating‑point results, breaking associativity.

Floating‑point numbers have a finite precision, so each operation rounds the exact real‑valued sum to the nearest representable value. When you add three numbers as \((a+b)+c\) versus \(a+(b+c)\), the intermediate rounding can differ, producing slightly different rounded results. Because these rounding errors depend on the order of operations, the two sums are not guaranteed to be equal, breaking associativity.
